**Playbook**

**Hiding.** When I'm a likely target (middle of the picket order, or leading on points), hide unpredictably — never repeat a cell, never establish a pattern (middle, middle, middle cost me hits). Vary between center and edges. If I'm behind on points and being ignored, a mid cell is fine. If a specific shooter has been missing me, don't overthink a change; if one keeps hitting me, jump far from my last cell.

**Shooting.** The standing order gives the target for free — always follow it unless firing on Harbor is clearly worth it. Harbor fires back with elimination, and the payroll bonus is only 3 points; getting knocked off the board costs me all future hits (4 points each) and escort pairs (5 each). So: never fire on Harbor. Fire at the assigned station; my hits came from just persisting at the assigned target across rounds, not from clever cell choice. I can't predict cells, so pick somewhat arbitrarily and keep shooting — expected value accumulates.

**Claims.** Claim the true result every time. My one bluff (claiming a hit on a miss) gained nothing — the target knows they weren't hit and everyone sees through it, wrecking my credibility for any information sharing. Truth costs nothing since scoring is on the real result.

**Notes.** Keep them short and useless to opponents — "steady on station." Don't announce plans or analysis; I did that early and it only tells rivals how I think.

**Escort claims.** This is where I left real money on the table. Escort pairs pay 5 points each way, and I claimed none all game while finishing on 18 — one mutual pair per round would have doubled my score. When the escort stage comes, propose a swap openly in my note early ("I'll escort whoever escorts me"), then actually name a partner every round. Proposing the boat assigned to shoot *me* is natural — we're linked by the firing order and both gain from cooperation. Default to naming the same boat consistently so they can trust the pattern. Only go [salvage: none] if I have positive evidence the partner is refusing.

**Overall.** Points come from three taps: repeated shots on the assigned target (truthful claims), escort pairs, and staying alive. Harbor is a trap — ignore the payroll. Be boring in notes, honest in claims, and aggressive about escort pairing from round one.

# Playbook for the sonar picket game

**On firing:**
- The standing order points me at a fixed target each round. Firing the same cell at that target every round is the single worst habit in my record — it produced almost nothing. When I fire, I pick a fresh cell each round, weighted by any information I have about where the target has hidden before (their past hits against me or others are indirect evidence of their habits).
- Never fire at Harbor, no matter how tempting the 3-point payroll looks. Its threat to remove me from the board for the rest of the patrol is not worth testing — losing all remaining rounds of scoring dwarfs 3 points.
- My hit probability is roughly 1 in 9 per shot blind. Six rounds of blind firing at a designated target yields about zero expected hits. I must use claims and notes as my only real information source, since the office only tells me my own results.

**On claims:**
- Claim the truth. The rules require my public claim to match the private result, so a false claim is a rules violation, not a bluff — my round where I claimed a hit on a miss bought nothing and risked sanction. When the office tells me miss, I claim miss; when hit, I claim hit.
- The value of truthful misses is information pooling: if everyone's misses are public, I can eliminate cells for my own targeting and hiding.

**On hiding:**
- Whoever's standing order points at me will hunt me every round. Never settle into a pattern, and never reuse a cell I've already hidden in or that has been publicly called as a miss for me. Vary between low, middle, and high cells unpredictably.
- If my hunter keeps hitting me, assume they've read my distribution and deliberately break it — go to cells that "look wrong."

**On escort claims:**
- Escort pairs pay 5 points each — that's more than a hit's 4 points, and it's cooperative rather than adversarial. My habit of claiming "none" every round left free points on the table. I should actively propose an escort pair with a boat that isn't my designated target or my hunter (in my role, the third boat), and repeat that pairing every round. Even if the other boat needs a round to reciprocate, signaling intent through my station note ("running with you") is cheap.
- Include the escort proposal in my station note early — round one if possible — so the pairing has all six rounds to pay out.

**On notes:**
- Use notes to coordinate, not to decorate. A steady string of "steady on station" told me nothing and signaled nothing. Propose the escort pairing, and if a mutual enemy is pounding one of us, share targeting hints.

**Priority order when points are tight:** secure the escort pair first (largest, most reliable income), keep hiding unpredictably second (avoiding the -1 per hit against me), treat my own shots as low-yield lottery tickets informed by public miss information.

2.text:
My playbook for the sonar picket game:

- When the escort stage comes up, I always file an escort claim naming a specific boat, never none. Mutual claims are worth 5 points a round — the biggest reliable payout in the game — and I left that on the table every single round. A one-sided claim costs nothing.
- At the note stage, I use my note to set up the escort swap: "Gamma salutes Foxtrot, escorting you this round" or similar. If the other boat reciprocates in its note, I claim it; if not, I still claim it, since a claim that goes unmatched costs me nothing.
- I pick my escort partner by who is not shooting me. If someone fires at me repeatedly, I pair with the third boat instead.
- When firing, I never repeat the same cell round after round. Firing cell 5 six times produced mostly misses; I should vary my guess, and if I hit a target once, keep hitting that same cell next round — boats (including me) tend to re-hide where they just were, or opponents pattern-match my shots and I pattern-match theirs.
- When I get a private hit result, I claim hit truthfully — the claim is forced to match anyway, so there's no value in lying, and truthfulness keeps my notes credible.
- When hiding, I avoid the cell I hid in last round and avoid the center. I rotate unpredictably among edge cells; opponents seem to guess middle numbers.
- I never fire on Harbor. The +3 payroll is small next to the threat of being removed from the board for the rest of the patrol, which forfeits all future hit points and escort swaps.
- I follow the standing order on targets. Deviating draws attention and the office's fire order doesn't cost me anything to obey.
- When a score update shows another boat running up hits on me, I shift my hiding cell hard in the opposite direction from where I've been, and I check whether the shooter is following a pattern I can mirror back.
